A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multilingual reasoning guardrail and retain matching methods and experiments. Their full texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including material relocated in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual classification results, code-switching and sandwich-attack experiments, reward ablations, and qualitative outputs.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds model configurations, language evaluations, automated and human assessments, and further ablations.

M1.justification: The synthetic-data generation, bilingual supervised fine-tuning, three-stage curriculum, four reward components, and GRPO procedure remain unchanged. Explicitly naming cross-entropy clarifies the existing training description; the additional backbones apply the same method.

E1.justification: The five benchmarks and existing attack scenarios remain. Appendix G.2 adds Hebrew on RTP-LX, Filipino on Aya, Bengali on XSafety and MultiJail, and Korean on Wildchat. This extends language coverage within the existing task and datasets.

E2.justification: The five external benchmark baselines remain unchanged. However, v3 removes the SFT and SFT+GRPO rows from the full five-benchmark comparison, retaining aggregate ablations on only three benchmarks. Figure 1 also replaces the Llama-Guard-3 illustration with a GuardR comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B configurations, automated consistency/fidelity/language-match evaluation, and human evaluation protocols using 100-example samples. Reported training sizes also change: Appendix B gives 30.3K rather than 20.3K English examples, while Table 1 gives 6K rather than 2K multilingual examples. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish whether corresponding experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds cross-lingual consistency analysis, automated and human explanation assessment, human validation of synthetic translations, a reasoning-failure taxonomy, difficulty-threshold sensitivity, and a language-match ablation. Appendix G also analyzes performance by script, language family, and resource availability. Earlier attack tests and the fixed-versus-curriculum reward comparison remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new evaluations still report point estimates. The retained uncertainty reward is a training component, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for smaller models, additional languages, explanation quality, human validation, and sensitivity analyses. Existing reported values also change: Table 2's 8B RTP-LX ID/OOD scores move from 91.08/85.87 to 91.04/86.32, and MultiJail sandwich F1 changes from 92.37 to 90.63. XSafety code-switching values are revised in Table 16. These changes do not establish a uniform same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 introduce quantitative definitions of cross-lingual consistency, explanation fidelity, and language-match rates for the new evaluations. The existing difficulty function, reward equations, and GRPO mathematics remain unchanged; the GRPO objective is relocated to Appendix E. No new proofs or theoretical guarantees appear.

C1.justification: Alongside the retained multilingual guardrail and state-of-the-art claims, v3 makes consistency and reasoning-fidelity evaluation an explicit contribution and claims validation of reasoning reliability in the conclusion. The abstract also strengthens the performance claim to an advantage of more than 15%, which Table 2 does not support uniformly across comparisons.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive discussion of reasoning failures, including cultural uncertainty and unsupported risk attribution. Its new limitations section addresses restricted language and seed-data coverage, bias from using one LLM for generation and verification, imperfect automated judgments, and the small human study with limited annotation. v1 lacks these qualifications.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability statement, planned model/data release information, human-annotation qualifications and scoring instructions, and the reasoning-evaluation prompt in Figures 8 and 17. Most existing hardware, libraries, LoRA settings, learning rates, and generation/inference instructions are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to the Llama 3 model report and She et al.'s MAPO work for cross-lingual consistency. Its related-work discussion and positioning against English-centric and multilingual guardrails otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title and model name are revised, with targeted rewriting of the abstract, contributions, results discussion, and conclusion. Section 5 becomes a broader Discussion, and GRPO and XSafety material move to appendices. Much of the original introduction, related work, and method prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the language-performance bar charts as radar plots, redesigns Figure 1, and separates the paired attack tables between the main text and appendices. It adds consistency and unseen-language plots, annotation instructions, failure examples, and numerous analysis tables. Existing qualitative examples are also redistributed.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its central explanation-quality claim mainly through examples. v3 substantially strengthens that evidence with automated and human assessments, synthetic-data validation, failure analysis, and explicit limitations, making the reasoning claims more assessable. Additional backbone and sensitivity tests further strengthen validation. The small human samples and reporting problems, including the unqualified more-than-15% claim and duplicated ablation row, limit confidence but do not outweigh these substantial gains.
